value.overview: The Long-tailed Silky-flycatcher is a striking montane bird of Costa Rica and western Panama. It has a glossy black head, bright yellow belly, gray back, and a long graduated tail. Usually seen in pairs or small groups, it occupies cool highland forests, forest edges, and open wooded areas. Its broad, rounded wings and strong bill suit a fruit-based diet, although it also takes insects, especially when feeding young.
value.classification: The Long-tailed Silky-flycatcher belongs to the silky-flycatcher family Ptiliogonatidae and the genus Ptiliogonys. It is one of two silky-flycatcher species found in Costa Rica.
value.identification: Adults have a black head and upper breast, a gray back, dark wings, and vivid yellow underparts. The long, narrow tail is mostly dark and gives the species its name. The sexes are similar, although females may appear slightly duller. Its combination of a yellow belly, dark head, gray upperparts, and exceptionally long tail distinguishes it from the smaller Black-and-yellow Silky-flycatcher. It is generally recognized by its deliberate flight and frequent upright perching in exposed branches.
value.rangeHabitat: The Long-tailed Silky-flycatcher occurs from Costa Rica south through western Panama and is strongly associated with high elevations. In Costa Rica it is widespread in the central and southern highlands, including montane regions and highland valleys, where it can occur in cloud forest, high-elevation evergreen forest, woodland borders, gardens, and other partly open habitats. It is often found from roughly 1,500 meters upward, with local elevations varying by mountain range and habitat conditions.
value.migrationStatus: It is primarily resident in Costa Rica rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may move locally or seasonally along mountain slopes, and birds can descend to lower elevations after breeding or when food availability changes.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs mainly during the rainy season, when fruit and insects are more available. The female builds a small cup-shaped nest, usually placed in a tree or shrub and concealed among foliage. Clutches generally contain a few eggs. Both adults participate in caring for the young, and the male commonly remains near the nest or helps supply food. Exact nesting dates and success vary among elevations and regions in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: Fruit forms an important part of the diet, including berries and other small fleshy fruits from native trees and shrubs. The species also catches insects and other small arthropods, particularly during the breeding season. It usually feeds from perches, making short flights to pick fruit or seize prey, and may forage in pairs or small groups. Highland gardens and forest edges can provide useful feeding sites when natural fruiting vegetation is present.
value.behavior: Long-tailed Silky-flycatchers are active but not highly restless birds. They often perch conspicuously on bare twigs or the tops of trees, making short sallies for fruit or insects before returning to a perch. They commonly occur in pairs or family groups and may join mixed-species flocks outside the breeding period. Their calls are soft, varied notes, and their flight is direct, with the long tail clearly visible.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, but the species is not currently considered to be undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline for a threatened category.
